_comment: Short facts taken from the chapter the day page reads (CPDV). Keyed by book:chapter so the section stays with the reading, not a stale date.

items: Joseph brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to Jacob when he hears that his father is sick.
Jacob crosses his hands: the right hand rests on Ephraim, the younger, and the left on Manasseh, the elder.
Joseph tries to move the right hand onto the firstborn. Jacob refuses, and he sets Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Jacob calls his sons and speaks a word over each of the twelve.
Reuben, the firstborn, is called the beginning of his sorrow. Simeon and Levi are divided because of their violence.
Of Judah he says the scepter will not be taken away until the one who will be sent arrives, the expectation of the Gentiles.
Jacob is carried to Canaan and buried in the double cave Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre.
Joseph tells his brothers, “You devised evil against me. But God turned it into good,” so that many peoples would be saved.
Before he dies, Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to carry his bones with them when God visits them.
A new king arises over Egypt who is ignorant of Joseph.
The Hebrew midwives are named Shiphrah and Puah. They fear God and let the boys live.
Pharaoh then orders every newborn Hebrew son to be thrown into the river.
When his mother can no longer hide him, she lays Moses in a basket of bulrushes smeared with pitch and tar.
Pharaoh’s daughter finds the basket among the papyruses. Moses later flees to Midian and marries Zipporah.
Their son is named Gershom, “for I have been a newcomer in a foreign land.”
The Lord appears to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush that burns and is not burnt.
He calls, “Moses, Moses,” and says he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses hides his face.
When Moses asks his name, God says, “I AM WHO AM,” and tells him to say, “HE WHO IS has sent me to you.”
Moses says he is not eloquent. The Lord gives him Aaron, his brother, to speak for him.
On the way, Zipporah circumcises their son with a sharp stone and says, “You are a bloody spouse to me.”
Aaron meets Moses. They gather the elders, Aaron speaks the words of the Lord, and the people believe.
Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh that the Lord says, “Release my people.” Pharaoh answers that he does not know the Lord.
The king stops giving chaff for the bricks and still demands the same quota. The people have to gather straw themselves.
The foremen are scourged for missing the quota. They tell Moses and Aaron, “You have caused our odor to become foul before Pharaoh.”
The Lord tells Moses, “I am the Lord,” and says he has remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He promises to lead Israel out from the work house of the Egyptians and to take them as his people.
Moses explains this to the sons of Israel. They do not agree with him, because of their anguish of spirit and very difficult work.
Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent and devours the staffs of Pharaoh’s sorcerers.
The water of the river is struck and turned into blood. The fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink it.
The sorcerers do the same by their incantations. Seven days pass after the Lord strikes the river.
Frogs come up into the houses, bedrooms, beds, and ovens. Pharaoh begs for them to be taken away, then hardens his heart.
The sorcerers cannot bring forth the gnats and say, “This is the finger of God.”
Flies fill Egypt, but the land of Goshen, where the Lord’s people live, is spared.
Hail and fire fall on Egypt, greater than any since the nation was formed. Goshen is left untouched.
Moses stretches out his hands and the thunder and hail cease.
When Pharaoh sees that they have stopped, he adds to his sin and will not let the people go.
Locusts eat whatever the hail left. A west wind then casts them into the Red Sea, and not one remains.
Moses stretches out his hand and a darkness that can be felt covers Egypt for three days.
The sons of Israel have light where they live. Moses says not one hoof of the flocks will stay behind, because the animals are needed for the worship of the Lord.
There is one plague left. After it, Pharaoh will not merely let the people go. He will drive them out.
Every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh’s firstborn on the throne to the firstborn of the handmaid at the millstone, and the firstborn of the cattle.
Moses goes out from Pharaoh exceedingly angry. Among the sons of Israel, not even a dog will mutter.
The Passover lamb is eaten in haste, with waist girded, shoes on, and a staff in hand. It is the Lord’s Passover.
At midnight the Lord strikes every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh’s heir to the captive in prison, and every firstborn of the cattle.
Israel had lived in Egypt four hundred and thirty years. On that same day the army of the Lord departs.
Every firstborn that opens the womb, of men and of cattle, is to be sanctified to the Lord.
God does not lead them by the way of the Philistines. He leads them around by the desert next to the Red Sea.
Moses carries the bones of Joseph, as Joseph had made Israel swear. The Lord goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
Moses tells the people, “The Lord will fight on your behalf, and you will remain silent.”
Israel goes through the midst of the dried sea, with the water like a wall on the right and on the left.
The waters return over Pharaoh’s chariots and horsemen. Not one of the army that followed them into the sea is left.
Moses and the sons of Israel sing, “The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea.” Miriam takes a timbrel and leads the women.
At Marah the water is bitter. The Lord shows Moses a tree, and the water becomes sweet.
At Elim there are twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, and they camp beside the waters.
The Lord rains bread from heaven and tells them to gather only enough for each day, as a test.
On the sixth day they collect a double portion, two omers for each man, because the next day is the Sabbath rest.
Aaron stores one omer of manna in a vessel, kept in the sight of the Lord for the generations to come.
At Rephidim there is no water. Moses strikes the rock at Horeb and water comes out for the people to drink.
Amalek fights Israel there. When Moses lifts his hands, Israel prevails. When he lowers them, Amalek prevails.
Aaron and Hur hold up his hands until sunset. Moses builds an altar and names it “The Lord, my Exaltation.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, comes with Zipporah and their two sons to the wilderness.
Jethro rejoices over all the good the Lord has done for Israel and offers a holocaust.
He tells Moses to appoint able men who fear God as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
